newsitem.title: INDIA: India court acquits three in "sati" death case.
newsitem.headline: India court acquits three in "sati" death case.

text.p: An Indian court has acquitted three people charged with abetting the suicide of a woman who climbed on to her husband's funeral pyre in following an ancient custom, officials said on Sunday.

Social activists all over India had erupted in furore when Roop Kanwar, a 19-year old widow, performed "sati" or self-immolation on September 4, 1987, at Deorala village, some 250 km (156 miles) from New Delhi, in Rajasthan state.
Some 5,000 people had watched Kanwar die, and villagers swore she had sat calmly holding her dead husband's head on her lap and chanting prayers as flames consumed her.
But police had charged Kanwar's brother-in-law, Pushpendra Singh, of lighting the pyre and her father-in-law Sumer Singh of forcing her to commit sati.

Independent India had endorsed a British colonial ruling in outlawing "sati" around 150 years ago, but the incident in 1987 was supported by conservative Hindu leaders and their followers in the northwestern state.
The family of Mal Singh, Roop Kanwar's dead husband, was accused of abetting the act of sati.

"All the 37 witnesses who had given their statements in the court turned hostile as a result of which there were not adequate evidence to prove that she was forced onto the pyre and asked to committ sati," Shabhu Dayal Agarwal, government lawyer, told Reuters on Sunday.
In Rajasthan, many among the Rajputs, a warrior Hindu caste to which Roop Kanwar belonged, see sati as a holy custom.
